events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. events.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety
events.title: Enmo Safety: External, Non-invasive, Model-agnostic Oversight for Off-the-Shelf Language Models

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform complex tasks using high-privilege tools, making indirect prompt injection (IPI) a critical security risk. However, IPI benchmarks lag behind their rapidly evolving utility counterparts, only offering limited task and environment coverage and relying on narrow, static attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose meta-benchmarking for IPI: transforming existing utility benchmarks into end-to-end IPI evaluation suites that reuse their realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure. We present MetaPI, an extensible toolkit that automatically identifies plausible injection points, generates realistic attack objectives, optimizes adaptive payloads, and validates attacks in the real environment. Its modular interfaces support heterogeneous environments, agents, defenses, and attack algorithms, allowing new components to be integrated without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We apply MetaPI to AppWorld, VitaBench, and Terminal-Bench and evaluate representative agents and defenses across multiple backbone LLMs. Our results show that no evaluated defense simultaneously achieves strong utility and strong security in realistic, adaptive agentic IPI settings. MetaPI thus enables scalable and consistent security evaluation across diverse and evolving agent ecosystems
events.title: MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10684v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.
events.title: Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realizing federated learning (FL) in remote regions lacking reliable cellular infrastructure is challenging, as it requires dependable communication among participating devices. Low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) offer an attractive communication solution for such scenarios. However, their limited data rates necessitate careful investigation of the communication-learning trade-offs and mechanisms to reduce communication overhead. This paper presents an investigation of the Long Range (LoRa) LPWAN technology for FL-based structural health monitoring (SHM), a representative remote IoT application. We consider a SCAFFOLD-based FL framework for multi-class anomaly detection and analyze the latency-accuracy trade-off. We also examine strategies for allocating the LoRa spreading factor (SF) during model-update exchange. Numerical results show that, with appropriate SF allocation, LoRa-supported FL-SHM can achieve competitive learning accuracy. In particular, jointly accounting for link distances and clients' dataset sizes when selecting the SF provides a favorable balance between convergence performance and communication latency. These preliminary findings offer useful insights into the design of FL systems over LPWANs for remote IoT deployments.
events.title: Federated learning for remote IoT over LPWAN: Preliminary insights from structural health monitoring

events.excerpt: arXiv:2505.12750v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Malware are malicious programs that are grouped into families based on their penetration technique, source code, and other characteristics. Classifying malware programs into their respective families is essential for building effective defenses against cyber threats. Machine learning models have a huge potential in malware detection on mobile devices, as malware families can be recognized by classifying permission data extracted from Android manifest files. Still, the malware classification task is challenging due to the high-dimensional nature of permission data and the limited availability of training samples. In particular, the steady emergence of new malware families makes it impossible to acquire a comprehensive training set covering all the malware classes. In this work, we present a malware classification system that, on top of classifying known malware, detects new ones. In particular, we combine an open-set recognition technique developed within the computer vision community, namely MaxLogit, with a tree-based Gradient Boosting classifier, which is particularly effective in classifying high-dimensional data. Our solution turns out to be very practical, as it can be seamlessly employed in a standard classification workflow, and efficient, as it adds minimal computational overhead. Experiments on public and proprietary datasets demonstrate the potential of our solution, which has been deployed in a business environment.
events.title: Malware families discovery via Open-Set Recognition on Android manifest permissions

During a weekend briefing , NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith. Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components. Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics." The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital. "You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said. For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said. "The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. events.excerpt: Overview Note This is an optional release for all op-supernode operators. It removes op-node's sequencer.max-safe-lag option from the virtual nodes, and updates golang.org/x/net past two advisories that do not affect op-supernode. Breaking changes Virtual-node sequencer.max-safe-lag flags removed ( #23738 ). Sequencing no longer pauses when the unsafe head runs ahead of the safe head. Remove --vn.all.sequencer.max-safe-lag and --vn.<chainID>.sequencer.max-safe-lag from the launch configuration before upgrading, because op-supernode rejects them as unknown flags. The OP_SUPERNODE_VN_ALL_SEQUENCER_MAX_SAFE_LAG and OP_SUPERNODE_VN_<chainID>_SEQUENCER_MAX_SAFE_LAG environment variables are no longer read. The option was disabled by default, so a supernode that never set it is unaffected. Other changes Update golang.org/x/net to v0.62.0, which fixes CVE-2026-78661 and CVE-2026-97045 ( #23728 ). Both are in the module's html package, which op-supernode does not use, so earlier releases were not affected; the update clears vulnerability-scanner findings against the module. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwards it to an implementation that interprets and executes it.
